Under "Protostomes," it reads "Protostomes include phyla such as arthropods, mollusks, and annelids. Mouth develops first." The accompanying diagram shows how the mouth develops as the first opening of the gut for these organisms. The next line says "Deuterostomes include the chordates and echinoderms. Under "Sponges," it says, "No symmetry, tissues, or organs. Flattened cells line the body wall (many pores; spikes of silica and/or proteins). Zygote develops into free-living larva." A diagram of the basic sponge body plan is on the right, showing its various parts. A photo of a yellow sponge is shown on the right of the bullet points. The video segment presents information about different types of worms. The speaker discusses Cnidarians (Phylum Cnidaria), explaining that they include jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones, found in aquatic environments. The text on the screen lists their characteristics: radial, tentacled carnivores, bag-like with one opening, having a gastrovascular cavity, true epithelial tissues with mesoglea, simple nervous system (nerve net), and hydrostatic skeleton. Some are commercial, and some are symbiotic with algae. The slide features illustrations of a nematocyst and an image of a sea anemone, with text indicating it's eaten by molluscs and flatworms as nematodes in the food web. A subsequent slide introduces "Unique Cnidarian Weapons" like nematocysts, used to capture prey and for defense, alongside a photo of a red jellyfish against a blue background. The video then shifts to Flatworms (Phylum Platyhelminthes), characterized as free-living turbellarians (planarians), parasitic tapeworms, and flukes. They are described as the simplest animals with organ systems, bilateral protostomes, with paired nerve cords and ganglia, and hermaphrodites. This slide features diagrams and images of different flatworms. Finally, Nematodes, also called roundworms, are introduced as parasitic creatures with tapered bodies at both ends, having a complete digestive system, chitin as an external skeleton, and a non-specialized excretory system. They are either monoecious or dioecious. An image depicts a nematode and its internal structure.
